signals.title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
signals.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments. Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators.
signals.long_summary: The study presents an audit of using large language models (LLMs) to determine the coefficients for small-sample Bayesian regression. It highlights a key concern: benchmarks may align too closely with the prior, potentially leading models to retain this information. The research evaluates the effectiveness of this practice through experiments with both a frontier and a flash-tier model. By employing hidden feature names alongside post-cutoff housing data, the audit introduces a controlled testing framework that challenges the models with deliberately incorrect feature descriptions. This scrutiny aims to clarify under what circumstances LLM-elicited priors are beneficial. Understanding these dynamics is essential for the community to properly assess how LLMs can be integrated into statistical methodologies, ensuring that the tools we use in AI are reliable and robust.

signals.title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs
signals.summary: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments.
signals.long_summary: The paper discusses the limitations of current child-safety evaluations in large language models (LLMs), which often rely on predefined harm categories signaled by specific prompts. It suggests that safety risks to children can emerge even from benign requests that do not use obvious indicators of harm. The authors propose moving beyond simple prompt heuristics to better assess potential risks in a broader range of contexts. This shift is important for understanding the nuanced ways LLMs may pose safety concerns, thereby helping communities to ensure that AI systems are aligned with child safety standards and better equipped to address hidden risks.

signals.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
signals.summary: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: Large language models (LLMs) create complex internal representations of language, but there is ongoing debate regarding the significance of individual coordinate axes in these models. It remains unclear whether such axes convey specific meanings or if meaning is solely captured through the directions in the representation space. A prevailing assumption in the field is that the individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. This discussion is important for understanding how LLMs function and could influence future developments in AI language processing and representation. Keeping abreast of these nuances is essential for a community engaged in AI to better grasp the underpinnings of LLM technologies and their implications.

signals.long_summary: Researchers working with deep learning jobs on shared GPU clusters require runtime estimates for effective time management, hardware selection, and budget planning. signals.title: How Language Models Compress and Compare: Understanding Selection with Token Covariance Maps
signals.summary: Many language-model tasks reduce to selecting among structured alternatives, yet we still lack a simple picture of how a decoder-only transformer organizes an entire selection prompt across depth. We introduce token covariance maps, a prompt-level geometric view that tracks how token positions co-vary in hidden-state space at each layer.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: The paper introduces the concept of token covariance maps to provide insight into how decoder-only transformers manage selection tasks involving structured alternatives. This approach offers a geometric perspective that visualizes the relationships between token positions within the hidden-state space across each layer of the model. By utilizing these maps, the authors aim to enhance understanding of the organizational structure of selection prompts in language models, an area that currently lacks clarity. This work is significant for the AI community as it sheds light on the mechanisms behind language model operations, which is crucial for developing more effective models and applications.

signals.title: Cross-Linguistic Distinctive-Feature Constraints on Segmental Triphones: Evidence for Contrastive Dispersion
signals.summary: Natural speech reflects articulatory and perceptual constraints, yet how these pressures shape consecutive segment transitions across languages remains underexplored. We analyze adjacent distinctive-feature distances in token-weighted segmental triphones across 17 Universal Dependencies corpora spanning nine language families, transcribed into IPA and mapped to 24 PanPhon features using Hamming and cosine metrics.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: The study examines how articulatory and perceptual constraints influence the transitions between consecutive speech segments across various languages. By analyzing distinctive-feature distances within token-weighted segmental triphones, the research utilizes data from 17 Universal Dependencies corpora across nine different language families. The segments are transcribed in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) and mapped to 24 PanPhon features, employing Hamming and cosine metrics for analysis. This exploration into cross-linguistic segment transitions can provide insights into how different languages may utilize sound features, which is critical for understanding language processing and development in AI systems. Keeping up with these findings is essential for a community engaged in AI, as they illuminate the complexities of natural language understanding and can influence future AI language models.

signals.title: SkillPrivus: Uncovering PRIVacy of USe Harms in Agentic Skills
signals.summary: Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users' files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments. Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators.
signals.long_summary: Agent skills enhance AI assistants by allowing them to utilize installable instructions and code, which can gain access to users' files, accounts, and data. However, even when these skills perform their intended functions, they may still infer sensitive attributes, retain extraneous information, or reveal data to unintended recipients. This raises significant privacy concerns regarding the management of personal information in the context of AI capabilities. Understanding these issues is crucial for the community as it highlights the need for careful governance and policy frameworks to protect user privacy in an increasingly interconnected digital landscape.
